To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the backdoor learned by the classifier is different from the trigger image, and 2) anyone with access to a poisoned classifier can easily construct alternative triggers that are just as effective or more effective in eliciting the target label at test time.
“Poisoned classifiers have backdoors that are not only backdoor-able, but can be backdoored by anyone with access to them.”

“backdoors in classifiers are not secret, and can be discovered by anyone with access to a classifier.” We hope that our work will help raise awareness about the fundamental flaws in the notion of secret backdoors, and that it will inspire the research community to develop new defenses that are more resilient to such attacks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether backdoors in machine learning models are truly “secret”, and we find that the answer is a resounding “no”.

the following questions: How do we detect the existence of backdoors in a classifier? How do we construct triggers that are effective against backdoored classifiers? How can we prevent backdoors from being constructed in the first place?
the question “how do poisoned models work?” We show that the answer is “not as intended”.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the notion of “backdoor” in poisoned classifiers is a misnomer.
the existence of backdoors is not a secret, and it can be discovered by anyone who has access to the classifier.
“poisoned classifiers are broken”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) we show that the trigger image itself is not necessary for backdoor attack; (2) our attack can be performed without the original training data; (3) we demonstrate the effectiveness of the attack on both TrojAI and ImageNet datasets; (4) our attack is robust to the denoising algorithm and can be applied to both the black-box and white-box settings.
we show that backdoored classifiers are not only vulnerable to the adversary that possesses the trigger but also to anyone who can get access to the poisoned classifier.
1. Poisoned classifiers are not “backdoors”, they are “broken doors”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
poisoned classifiers are not just vulnerable to backdoor attacks, but fundamentally broken, and thus cannot be trusted in any security-critical setting.
poisoned classifiers are fundamentally broken, and should never be deployed.
the notion of “backdoor” as a “secret trigger” is fundamentally flawed.
